title: Prosecutor v. Jean-Pierre Bemba Gombo — command responsibility
question: Has it been established beyond reasonable doubt that the commander of a force deployed in a foreign country was criminally responsible under Article 28(a) of the Rome Statute for crimes committed by that force's troops?
facts: Troops of the Mouvement de libération du Congo (MLC) operated in the Central African Republic from on or about 26 October 2002 to 15 March 2003. The Trial Chamber found the commander to have acted as a military commander with effective control over the troops. The crimes at issue included murder, rape, and pillaging. On appeal he argued that the Trial Chamber had misappreciated the limitations of the MLC's jurisdiction and competence to investigate, and that it had ignored that he had asked the Central African Republic Prime Minister to investigate the allegations and had sent a letter to the Central African Republic authorities concerning allegations of crimes. Evidence before the Trial Chamber included testimony about the limits of his power to investigate crimes committed in the Central African Republic and about logistical difficulties in doing so, and the MLC relied on cooperation with the Central African Republic authorities during the operation. The Trial Chamber acknowledged that he had taken some measures during the operation, while the dissenting judges described the Trial Chamber's assessment as finding those measures limited in mandate, execution, or results. The Trial Chamber found that MLC troops continued committing crimes throughout the operation and that consistent information about these crimes was brought to his attention. He initiated inquiries. Other MLC commanders exercised some disciplinary authority in the field.
holding: In its Appeals Judgment of 8 June 2018, the ICC Appeals Chamber majority found that errors materially affected the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the commander had failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures under Article 28 of the Rome Statute. The majority held that he could not be held criminally liable under Article 28 for the crimes committed by MLC troops during the operation, reversed his conviction, discontinued proceedings for acts outside the scope of the charges, and acquitted him of the remaining criminal acts. Judges Monageng and Hofmański dissented and would have confirmed the Trial Chamber's conviction.
key_reasoning: The Appeals Chamber majority identified errors in the assessment of the commander's ability to investigate and prosecute crimes in a foreign country and the evidence about cooperation with local authorities.
The majority found that the Trial Chamber had not addressed the commander's argument that he sent a letter to the Central African Republic authorities concerning allegations of crimes.
The majority found errors in the assessment of inquiries initiated by the commander, the role of other MLC officials, the number of crimes proved, and troop redeployment as a measure.

The Appeals Chamber majority concluded that these errors materially affected the finding that the commander failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures and entered an acquittal on the remaining criminal acts.
